what_it_does: Large cloud platforms run thousands of microservices — small, specialized programs that handle one narrow task (authentication, payment, recommendation) and talk to each other over a network. When hardware fails or demand spikes suddenly, the cloud operator needs to shed load fast while keeping the most important services alive. Today this is done manually or with blunt rules, risking either dropping critical services or keeping unimportant ones running at the expense of the overall cluster. Phoenix lets developers label each container (the packaged unit each microservice runs in) as either critical or non-critical. During a capacity crisis, Phoenix applies what it calls 'diagonal scaling': it automatically shuts down non-critical containers to free up the compute resources those containers were using, directing that capacity toward keeping critical containers healthy. An orchestration layer built on top of Kubernetes (the standard cloud container management system) jointly optimizes for the application's own criticality rules and the operator's infrastructure goals at the same time. According to the abstract, Phoenix can respond to failures across a 100,000-node cluster in about 10 seconds.
